source_evidence.anchor: [E1] “A function ψ : [0, ∞) → [0, ∞) is called an Orlicz function”
source_evidence.observation: The source requires ψ to be convex and increasing, with ψ(0) = 0 and ψ(x) tending to infinity as x tends to infinity.

source_evidence.location: First edition (2018), PDF page 24 / printed page 35, §2.7.1, paragraph beginning “For a given Orlicz function ψ”
source_evidence.observation: For a random variable X, the functional is ∥X∥ψ := inf {t > 0 : E ψ(|X|/t) ≤ 1}.

source_evidence.location: First edition (2018), PDF page 24 / printed page 35, §2.7.1, paragraph beginning “The Orlicz space Lψ”

source_evidence.observation: Lψ consists of all random variables X on the probability space (Ω, Σ, P) whose Orlicz functional is finite.

binders: A fixed function ψ : [0, ∞) → [0, ∞) satisfying the Orlicz-function conditions [E1].
A fixed probability space (Ω, Σ, P) [E3].

Random variables X and Y in Lψ, and a scalar a, when the word “norm” in the exercise is unpacked into its axioms; these binders are implicit in the norm assertion rather than separately displayed in the exercise [E3, E4].
hypotheses: For X and Y under consideration, ∥X∥ψ < ∞ and ∥Y∥ψ < ∞, because they belong to Lψ [E3].
conclusions: The explicitly requested conclusion is that X ↦ ∥X∥ψ defines a norm on Lψ [E4].
Unpacking “norm” requires nonnegativity and definiteness: ∥X∥ψ ≥ 0, and ∥X∥ψ = 0 exactly when X is zero in the applicable random-variable equality convention [E2, E4; norm-axiom expansion].
Unpacking “norm” requires absolute homogeneity: ∥aX∥ψ = |a| ∥X∥ψ for every scalar a [E2, E4; norm-axiom expansion].
Unpacking “norm” requires the triangle inequality: ∥X + Y∥ψ ≤ ∥X∥ψ + ∥Y∥ψ [E2, E4; norm-axiom expansion].

The assertion that this is a norm on Lψ also entails that Lψ supports the relevant vector-space operations; in particular, the displayed homogeneity and triangle inequality imply closure under scalar multiplication and addition for finite-norm variables [E3, E4; structural consequence of the norm assertion].
Completeness of Lψ is not required by Exercise 2.7.11; the source states it separately as an additional fact [E5].
definitions_and_conventions: Orlicz function: ψ : [0, ∞) → [0, ∞), convex and increasing, with ψ(0) = 0 and ψ(x) → ∞ as x → ∞ [E1].
Orlicz space: Lψ = Lψ(Ω, Σ, P) := {X : ∥X∥ψ < ∞}, where X ranges over random variables on (Ω, Σ, P) [E3].
The threshold in the defining expectation inequality is exactly 1, and the infimum ranges over strictly positive real t [E2].
The definition uses an infimum, not a stated minimum; attainment at t = ∥X∥ψ is not asserted [E2].

The absolute value and division by t are applied pointwise to X, and E is expectation with respect to P; this is the standard reading of the notation in the fixed probability-space context [E2, E3; implicit notation].
implicit_context: The functional is considered only on finite-norm random variables when proving it is a norm [E3, E4].
The exercise introduces no independence, centering, integrability-moment, or distributional hypotheses beyond membership in Lψ and the stated conditions on ψ [E1–E4].
The individual norm axioms are not printed separately; they are inherited from the standard mathematical meaning of “is indeed a norm” [E4].

Equality of random variables must be interpreted modulo almost-sure equality for definiteness to hold as a genuine norm; the selected passage does not state this convention explicitly [E3, E4; necessary standard convention].

details: The claim applies for each fixed Orlicz function ψ satisfying all four conditions in [E1] and for random variables in the associated Lψ on the fixed probability space [E3, E4].
The norm axioms quantify over all X, Y ∈ Lψ and all scalars of the underlying random-variable vector space [E4; norm-axiom expansion].
The exact gauge condition is E ψ(|X|/t) ≤ 1, with t > 0 [E2].
Changing the threshold, replacing ≤ by <, or omitting the absolute value would change the displayed source definition [E2].
The norm claim is restricted to Lψ, whose membership condition is finiteness of the displayed infimum [E3, E4].
The source does not claim that every random variable on (Ω, Σ, P) has finite Orlicz norm [E3].
On random variables viewed modulo almost-sure equality, definiteness means ∥X∥ψ = 0 if and only if X = 0 almost surely [E3, E4; necessary interpretation of the norm assertion].
On literal pointwise functions, a nonzero function supported on a P-null set has the same functional as zero, so the assertion would yield only a seminorm [E2–E4; analyst consequence].
Convexity is an explicit Orlicz-function hypothesis [E1] and is the source condition relevant to the triangle inequality asserted implicitly by [E4].
The zero scalar and zero random variable are included in the standard homogeneity and definiteness requirements; the source states no exception for them [E2, E4; norm-axiom expansion].
No completeness conclusion is demanded by this exercise [E5].

undebatable_constraints: ψ must be convex and increasing [E1].
The functional must be the exact infimum inf {t > 0 : E ψ(|X|/t) ≤ 1} [E2].
The claimed norm is restricted to Lψ = {X : ∥X∥ψ < ∞} on the stated probability space [E3, E4].
A faithful expansion of the exercise must include definiteness, absolute homogeneity, and the triangle inequality, rather than merely finiteness or nonnegativity [E4; standard meaning of norm].
The exercise does not require proving completeness or the Banach-space conclusion [E5].

ambiguities.issue: The selected passage does not explicitly say whether random variables are literal measurable functions or equivalence classes modulo almost-sure equality.
ambiguities.evidence: Lψ is described simply as consisting of “all random variables X” on (Ω, Σ, P), while Exercise 2.7.11 calls the functional a norm [E3, E4].
ambiguities.impact: For a genuine norm, equality must be almost-sure equality (or variables must be quotient classes). On raw pointwise functions, the functional is only a seminorm because changes on null sets are invisible to expectation.

ambiguities.issue: The passage does not state whether “increasing” means nondecreasing or strictly increasing.
ambiguities.evidence: The Orlicz-function definition uses the unqualified word “increasing” [E1].
ambiguities.impact: This affects whether ψ may vanish on a nontrivial initial interval, although the remaining convexity and divergence conditions still support the intended norm claim under the almost-sure equality convention.

ambiguities.issue: The scalar field of the random-variable space is not restated in §2.7.1.
ambiguities.evidence: The passage specifies random variables on (Ω, Σ, P) and uses |X|, but it does not explicitly say “real” or “complex” vector space [E2, E3].
ambiguities.impact: The homogeneity axiom must quantify over whichever scalar field is intended; its form remains ∥aX∥ψ = |a|∥X∥ψ.

ambiguities.issue: No convention for the infimum of an empty admissible set is stated.
ambiguities.evidence: The functional is defined by an infimum in [E2], and Lψ is then defined by the condition that this value is finite [E3].
ambiguities.impact: The natural extended-real convention gives value +∞ outside the finite-norm domain, but the exercise itself avoids this issue by asserting the norm only on Lψ.

contract_plain_english: Fix an Orlicz function ψ and a probability space. For each random variable X, take the infimum of all t > 0 for which E ψ(|X|/t) ≤ 1, and let Lψ contain exactly the variables for which this value is finite [E1–E3]. Exercise 2.7.11 asks for proof that this functional satisfies all norm axioms on Lψ—definiteness, absolute homogeneity, and the triangle inequality, with closure of Lψ under the vector-space operations understood [E4]. The genuine-norm reading requires random variables to be identified up to almost-sure equality; otherwise the functional cannot distinguish functions differing only on null sets [E2–E4]. Completeness is explicitly mentioned only as an additional fact beyond the exercise [E5].
